question.prompt:
Using only the paths and the directions shown, how many different routes are there from \(M\) to \(N?\)

[Figure 1](figures/1986_AMC_8_Q09_question_fig1.svg)

solutions.explanation:
Every route must start by going from \(M\) to either \(A\) or \(B\). Separating these two possibilities helps us avoid counting a route twice.

After reaching \(A\), we can go directly to \(C\), or go through \(D\) to \(C\). From \(C\), the only next destination is \(N\). This gives two routes:
\[
\begin{aligned}
&M\to A\to C\to N,\\
&M\to A\to D\to C\to N.
\end{aligned}
\]
After reaching \(B\), we can go to \(N\), to \(C\), or to \(A\). The last possibility has the two continuations just described. Thus there are four routes starting with \(MB\):
\[
\begin{aligned}
&M\to B\to N,\\
&M\to B\to C\to N,\\
&M\to B\to A\to C\to N,\\
&M\to B\to A\to D\to C\to N.
\end{aligned}
\]
These lists include every allowed choice at each junction, and their sequences of paths are all different. Therefore there are \(2+4=\boxed{6}\) routes, choice \(\text{E}\).
solutions.title: List routes by their first path
